questions.q: Why isn't being filled automatically good news for a market maker?
options: Fills are bad news only when they happen during market holidays
A counterparty only trades against a quote when it looks good TO THEM -- a quote that looks unusually good to an informed trader is often one the fair-value estimate got slightly wrong
Being filled is always good news with no exceptions
Market makers are never actually filled, only liquidity takers are
questions.explain: Adverse selection means fills disproportionately come from informed counterparties right before the price moves unfavorably -- a direct consequence of how market making works, not bad luck.

questions.q: What does markout analysis actually measure?
options: How the price moved in the seconds or minutes after a fill, relative to the fill price -- a direct, after-the-fact measure of how costly that fill turned out to be
The bid-ask spread at the moment of the fill only
The total dollar volume traded by a market maker in a single day
The number of competing market makers quoting the same instrument
questions.explain: Markout specifically looks at post-fill price movement to assess, after the fact, whether a given fill (or pattern of fills) was adversely selected.

questions.q: In the lesson's corrected worked example, what does a mean markout of -0.0756 with 70.5% of fills negative actually indicate?
options: A calculation error, since markout should always be exactly zero
A real, quantifiable toxic-flow signal -- the price moves against the maker's position after most (not all) fills, more than a healthy pattern would show
That all 200 fills were unprofitable
A perfectly healthy market-making pattern with no cause for concern
questions.explain: A negative mean markout with a strong majority of fills negative (70.5%, not 100%) is the realistic signature of toxic flow -- most but not all fills move unfavorably, which is why this requires statistical measurement, not fill-by-fill judgment.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that ~30% of fills DO move favorably, rather than claiming all fills are toxic?
options: Because markout analysis is only valid when exactly 50% of fills are favorable
Because toxicity has to be measured statistically across many fills -- no single fill proves anything, but the aggregate pattern does
Because the 30% favorable fills prove the maker's flow is not actually toxic at all
Because this detail is irrelevant to understanding adverse selection
questions.explain: A realistic toxic-flow pattern is a majority-unfavorable distribution, not a deterministic one -- this is precisely why markout has to be analyzed in aggregate rather than judged fill-by-fill.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the practical defenses against adverse selection described in this lesson?
options: Permanently quoting the widest possible spread at all times, regardless of market conditions
Setting size limits per quote, since very large trades against a resting quote are more likely to be informed
Fade protection: reacting immediately to a burst of same-direction fills as a toxicity signal
Widening the spread around scheduled information events like earnings or economic data releases
questions.explain: The lesson's real defenses are targeted and conditional (widen around news, size limits, fade protection) -- permanently maximizing spread width isn't a defense, it's just abandoning the market-making business entirely.
